title: Sonja V. Vance-Abate Obituary - The Desert Sun
content: After years of health challenges, Sonja passed away peacefully at home, surrounded by her children. Sonja lived a life rich in creativity, adventure, and love. A talented interior designer, writer, producer, actor, and fabulous cook, she enjoyed golf, reading, traveling with loved ones, and exploring her family’s genealogy. Her fun-loving spirit and generous heart touched many lives, and her family and friends meant everything to her. Sonja is survived by her children, Robin Black, Ray Black, and Rhonda Black; stepchildren, Howard Vance (Mildred), Cheryl Hunter (James), and Mark Abate (Gloria); brother, John Mortensen (Marcia); sisters, Sandra Carr and Karen Law (Lou); grandchildren, Rachel Black and William Whitten; her step-grandchildren and great-grandchildren, as well as many extended family members and close friends. She was preceded in death by her husbands, Larry Black, George Vance, and Robert Abate; her parents Tage and Ruby Mortensen; sister, Mitzi Mortensen; her stepson, Gregory Vance; brother-in-law, James Carr; and nephew, David Mortensen, A Celebration of Life will be held in Spokane, Washington, in spring 2027. Sonja's detailed obituary can be found on Legacy.com. Coping with grief when a traditional funeral isn't possible

title: New BMW iX4 vs. Old X4: More Power, Less Familiarity - bmwblog
content: The electric iX4 brings a radical cabin redesign and 603 hp in M60 form. How much of the outgoing X4’s character survives? There was a time where we weren’t sure we’d ever see the BMW X4 again. But today marks its triumphant return, and with a seriously renewed lease on life. Chiefly, it’s an EV, joining the growing family of Neue Klasse vehicles. The new generation also debuts with the most powerful X4 ever made, with the quickest 0-60 mph time to boot—yes, that includes the wicked BMW X4 M. Anyway, here’s how the new iX4 stacks up against the classic G02 generation. BMW has finally done it: the new iX4 is only imperceptibly larger than the X4 it replaces. Yes, it’s still bigger—but hardly. The iX4 is just half an inch longer than the G02 X4, while gaining two inches (25 mm) in the wheelbase. It’s less than an inch wider, too, and actually stands half an inch shorter than the outgoing model. Aesthetically, the iX4 stays fairly true to the G02’s brief. The sloping hatch terminates in a subtle (or not-so-subtle in M60 versions) rear spoiler, and everything about the iX4 screams sporty. The iX4 offers larger 22-inch wheels than its predecessor, too. Aside from the bigger wheels, the changes are…well, obvious. The iX4 dons a completely new suit for its Neue Klasse generation. A higher beltline gives the new SUV a little bit more verticality than the outgoing model, and we’ll for sure miss the M mirrors from the outgoing M and M Performance models. Same goes for the little roof spoiler. The tail lights appear slightly larger here than on other Neue Klasse models, and overall the design is good, if a bit disconnected from the previous generation. One look inside makes it immediately clear which of the two models is the new one. The good news: leather is still optional, and it’s unlikely the new X4 loses much in the way of meaningful cargo or passenger space. On the other hand, the Neue Klasse steering wheel is likely going to be a “love it or hate it” affair on a driver-by-driver basis. The lack of real buttons and addition of haptic ones will also likely divide commenters and some buyers. The iX4 offers a panoramic glass roof, replacing the old X4’s smaller unit (which also opened…). Only time behind the wheel will really establish whether the new interior digs are an objective improvement. When we break down the numbers, the iX4 starts to get a lot more impressive—quickly. BMW says the new iX4 M60 xDrive develops 603 hp and 645 lb-ft of torque (450 kW and 875 Nm) which makes it the most powerful X4 ever. The runner-up is the previous generation X4 M Competition, which made a nice 503 horsepower and 479 lb-ft. The iX4 doesn’t break any records in the 0-60 mph time, though. BMW claims the 0-100 km/h (62 mph) dash takes 3.9 seconds. While faster times have been independently reported, BMW officially estimated the LCI’d X4 M Competition’s 0-100 km/h time at 3.8 seconds per the 2021 press release. Close but no cigar. Top speed is a different story: the iX4 tops out at 149 mph, while the F98 X4 M achieved speeds up to 285 km/h (178 mph). Aesthetically, there’s a lot of new in the iX4. But in practice little will change with the new generation. For example, both X4 models offer built in navigation, app integration, a powerful head up display, and wireless phone charging. Displays move around a bit—the Panoramic Display most prominently, as it replaces the driver’s side gauge cluster entirely—but it’s a lot of the same information. The iX4 gains AI-assisted voice commands which should make things a little bit more conversational. Overall the Neue Klasse cars represent a step forward in customization and app integration. So, what do you think? Is the iX4 an immediate and obvious step up? Or were you hoping for something else? While we certainly mourn the loss of the radical X4 M, there’s something to be said for the new NA7 and its insane balance of tech and performance.

title: BMW iX4 vs. Audi Q4 Sportback: Similar Shape, Very Different Numbers - bmwblog
content: BMW’s Neue Klasse coupe SUV brings bold styling and big performance claims. Here’s how it compares with Audi’s electric Sportback. The Audi and BMW rivalry continues. This time, we’re lining up the two brands’ controversial “Sport Activity Coupes.” Funny enough, both have now gone electric-only; meet the BMW iX4 and the Audi Q4 e-tron Sportback. These flashy “coupe SUVs” are often maligned for being more style than substance.  But after comparing the two, it’s clear at least one of these things has some serious staying power. Audi’s coupe SUV and BMW’s iX4 share the same less-than-conventional sloping rear end and lots of details that shout, rather than whisper, that “this is the sporty one.” In the front, you’d have a hard time telling the iX4 or the Audi Q4 e-tron Sportback apart from its generation/platform-mates. But both benefit from aggressive, blacked-out trim pieces that overall keep proportions looking good on both. Audi’s Singleframe grille is a bit more familiar than the Neue Klasse one, and its wider proportions along with more rounded surfaces keep the Audi’s front end looking a little bit burlier overall. BMW, meanwhile, favors slimmer sharper angles and slimmer details. Notably, Audi only offers the Q4 e-tron Sportback in four colors (or did in 2026, anyway); BMW offers nine. From the side and rear is where both SUVs really lean into their sportier selves. Both cars offer 21-inch wheels, although BMW lets you step up to 22-inchers on the M60 model. Similarly, the two share lightly flared fenders, a dynamic rear wing, and a sprinkling of gloss black where needed (i.e., rear diffusor and other trim pieces). Audi’s Sportback’s wheelbase stretches 108.7 inches (2,761.0 mm) long, while the vehicle itself sits at 180.7 inches (4,589.8 mm). It stands 63.5 inches (1,612.9 mm) tall. The X4 is measurably larger. Its wheelbase is 114.1 inches (2,898.1 mm), underpinning a vehicle stretching 188.3 inches (4,783 mm) long and standing 63.3 inches (1,608 mm) tall. The X4 is also about an inch wider. Inside, the Audi Q4 e-tron Sportback offers a couple of features that BMW drivers might miss. One is the large passenger screen, which BMW is not bringing to the iX4. Thankfully, both cars offer leather, and the cost will be around the same ($1500). One big point of contention might be the sunroof; Audi offers a sunroof that actually opens, unlike the full-length panoramic glass roof in the new BMW iX4. Overall, both vehicles offer a commensurately upscale cabin for the price point and segment. Historically, the X4 has offered very slightly less cargo space and cabin space (head room and leg room) than the Q4 e-tron Sportback despite its larger size. That likely rings true here, too. The most aggressive iteration of the Audi Q4 e-tron Sportback currently (no pun intended) tops out at 335 hp (250 kW). Torque is another story: the top dog sends 545 Nm to the rear wheels and up to 134 Nm to the front wheels (401 and 99 lb-ft, respectively). Solid numbers all around—especially for something that doesn’t have an S or RS badge. But the iX4 M60 xDrive handily bests the Audi here. BMW claims 603 hp and 645 lb-ft of torque; that’s 450 kW and 875 Nm. The iX4 dashes from zero to 62 mph in 3.9 seconds and tops out at 149 mph. The top Audi does the same feat in an estimated 5.4 seconds, although no top speed is specified. Both vehicles offer bidirectional charging. Audi’s 2026 Q4 Sportback e-tron offers an EPA-estimated 251 miles of range, but the automaker refreshed some hardware for the latest model year that will likely drive that number up to or well past 300 miles. However, it’s a bit of a moot point: the X4 50 xDrive offers a preliminary estimated range of up to 428 miles. That number could change after testing, but it likely won’t fluctuate enough to make the Audi competitive. The Audi and BMW are closer than ever when comparing technology features. Both offer AI-enhanced voice commands (Amazon Alexa+ in the iX4, ChatGPT in Audi) that allow “natural interaction.” Both offer built-in maps and OEM app features. Displays are a completely different story, though. Audi offers a 12-inch passenger screen, which the iX4 doesn’t. BMW’s Panoramic Vision delivers a lot of the same info Audi’s 11.9-inch digital instrument cluster offers, but on the windshield instead of backing the steering wheel. The BMW iX4 starts at $66,200 in the U.S., which means it will be a tad bit more expensive than Audi’s EV. But, frankly, it sure seems like you get a lot for the money. The new iX4 offers more power and significantly more range; and does so looking pretty good. Which would you take home?

title: Substantiation, Partner Basis, and Methodologies: An Analysis of West v. Commissioner - Current Federal Tax Developments
content: A site devoted to articles on current developments in federal taxes geared toward CPAs in tax practice. West v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2026-105, Oct. 7, 2026 The petitioner, Andrew B. West, was an entrepreneur involved in various commercial activities during the 2015 and 2016 taxable years, operating primarily in Texas. During these years, Mr. West owned three limited liability companies: MPC Equipment, LLC; ABW Equipment Rentals, LLC; and Tilden Operating Management, LLC. On his federal individual income tax returns (Forms 1040), Mr. West reported these business activities across three separate Schedules C: Schedule C-1 for “Management Services,” Schedule C-2 for “MPC Equipment LLC,” and Schedule C-3 for “ABW Equipment Rentals LLC.” In addition to his own entity operations, Mr. West was employed by Oscar Leo Quintanilla to manage Mr. Quintanilla’s extensive business interests, which spanned oil and gas, cattle operations, and real estate development. Under a 2011 employment agreement with Paloma Cattle Co. Ltd., Mr. West served as president and CEO of several Quintanilla-owned entities and was entitled to an “Operating Bonus” equal to 6% of aggregate business profits. The financial relationship between Mr. West and Mr. Quintanilla was highly intertwined and characterized by informal, centralized accounting. Mr. Quintanilla’s accountants managed a centralized bill-paying apparatus that paid expenses for Quintanilla entities as well as personal and business expenses incurred directly by Mr. West or his LLCs. Expenses paid on Mr. West’s behalf were centrally billed to him via intercompany invoices, which Mr. West then settled from his personal or LLC bank accounts. Under his employment agreement, Mr. West was entitled to full reimbursement for out-of-pocket expenses incurred on behalf of Quintanilla entities; the court found that this centralized payment structure ensured that reimbursable employment expenses were paid directly by Quintanilla entities and were not borne by Mr. West personally. On January 1, 2014, Mr. West and Mr. Quintanilla entered into a formal joint venture designated as the “Commodities Trading Partnership” to manage commodities trading accounts. The partnership was established through three executed instruments: a Commodity Trading Allocation Agreement (CTA), a Secured Promissory Note (CTA Note) capped at $5 million, and an All-Assets Security Agreement. Under the CTA terms, Mr. Quintanilla contributed 100% of the initial capital, while Mr. West contributed no capital, supplying only his labor and trading management services. Profits and losses were allocated 50% to each partner. Any net loss allocated to Mr. West at the annual December 31 settlement date was deemed automatically borrowed from Mr. Quintanilla under the CTA Note, secured by all of Mr. West’s personal and business assets. Over its 26-month existence prior to termination on February 26, 2016, the Commodities Trading Partnership incurred significant net losses. In 2014, the partnership sustained a net loss of $13,729,319 (all of which Mr. Quintanilla claimed on his 2014 return). In 2015, the partnership generated net gains of $2,563,150, followed by a net loss of $148,902 during early 2016. Aggregate partnership net losses totaled $11,315,071, yielding a 50% distributive share of loss to Mr. West equal to $5,657,536. In March 2015, while indebted under the CTA Note, Mr. West executed a Purchase Agreement (“2015 Asset Purchase Agreement”) selling approximately $4.5 million of his personal and LLC assets to Mr. Quintanilla. In lieu of cash proceeds, the agreement directed Mr. Quintanilla to satisfy various personal and business liabilities owed by Mr. West, including a $2.2 million post-nuptial note owed to his former spouse, Carey West. The assets sold had previously served as collateral under the CTA Note; however, the purchase agreement made no contractual reference to the CTA, the CTA Note, or the commodities trading venture. Following Mr. West’s termination in February 2016, extensive state court litigation ensued in the Bexar County District Court of Texas. In December 2021, the Texas state court determined that Mr. West remained personally liable to Mr. Quintanilla for $5,878,127 under the CTA Note and that this liability had neither been satisfied nor released by the 2015 asset sale. Upon examination of Mr. West’s 2015 and 2016 returns, the Internal Revenue Service performed a Bank Deposits Analysis (BDA) across three of Mr. West’s primary bank accounts at Jefferson Bank. The revenue agent identified $162,091 in unreported gross receipts for 2015 and disallowed approximately $1 million in aggregate Schedule C deductions across 16 categories for 2015 and 2016. On July 10, 2019, the IRS issued a statutory Notice of Deficiency (NOD) asserting tax deficiencies of $463,827 for 2015 and $5,831 for 2016, along with I.R.C. § 6662(a) accuracy-related penalties totaling $93,881 ($92,765 for 2015 and $1,116 for 2016). Mr. West timely petitioned the United States Tax Court under I.R.C. § 6213(a) seeking redetermination of the deficiencies and accuracy-related penalties. In an amended petition, Mr. West asserted that he was entitled to recognize an ordinary partnership loss deduction of $6.8 million (or $6,894,774) for tax year 2016 stemming from the termination of the Commodities Trading Partnership, and to carry back the unused portion of that loss to tax year 2015. Mr. West contended that this loss carryback would entirely eliminate his taxable income and result in zero tax deficiency for both 2015 and 2016. Regarding gross income, Mr. West challenged the Commissioner’s BDA determination, arguing that two specific bank deposits were non-taxable nontaxable reimbursements: a deposit of $115,870.52 (which he alleged was a repayment for a Porsche purchased for Mr. Quintanilla’s son) and a deposit of $50,000 (which he claimed represented an overpayment refund from Water Well Services). Regarding trade or business expenses under I.R.C. § 162, Mr. West sought to substantiate disallowed Schedule C deductions by submitting eight post-trial spreadsheets attached to his briefs, claiming deductible amounts that differed substantially from—and in many cases exceeded—the amounts originally claimed on his tax returns. In addition, Mr. West argued for two specific deductions arising from the proceeds of the 2015 Asset Purchase Agreement: a $187,114.62 payment to Quintanilla Management Company (QMC) as Schedule C-2 “Professional Services” and a $112,257.21 payment to Q-Haul, Inc. as Schedule C-1 “Repairs and Maintenance.” Finally, Mr. West asserted relief from I.R.C. § 6662(a) accuracy-related penalties under the reasonable cause and good faith exception of I.R.C. § 6664(c)(1). He argued that any recordkeeping deficiencies stemmed from his former partner’s hostility, unfulfilled federal subpoenas, and the IRS’s refusal to accept delivery of 27 boxes of documents tendered during litigation. The United States Tax Court, with Judge Gustafson presiding, systematically evaluated the evidentiary framework, statutory requirements, and substantive tax provisions governing each disputed issue. Under Tax Court Rule 142(a) and established precedent in Welch v. Helvering, 290 U.S. 111, 115 (1933), the Commissioner’s deficiency determinations are presumed correct, placing the burden of proof squarely on the taxpayer to substantiate entitlement to claimed deductions (INDOPCO, Inc. v. Commissioner, 503 U.S. 79, 84 (1992)). While I.R.C. § 7491(a) can shift the burden of proof to the Commissioner under specified circumstances, Mr. West did not assert or satisfy the threshold requirements of section 7491(a). In unreported income cases, the Commissioner must establish an initial evidentiary foundation connecting the taxpayer with the income-producing activity (Llorente v. Commissioner, 649 F.2d 152, 156 (2d Cir. 1981)) or demonstrate actual receipt of funds (Edwards v. Commissioner, 680 F.2d 1268, 1270–71 (9th Cir. 1982)). Once established, the burden shifts to the taxpayer to demonstrate that the determination is arbitrary or erroneous (Walker v. Commissioner, 757 F.2d 36, 38 (3d Cir. 1985)). Addressing procedural mechanics, Judge Gustafson strictly enforced evidentiary boundaries regarding post-trial submissions. Under Niedringhaus v. Commissioner, 99 T.C. 202, 214 n.7 (1992), evidence must be formally introduced at trial; taxpayers cannot supplement the evidentiary record through post-trial brief attachments. Consequently, the court explicitly refused to consider several hundred pages of unadmitted invoices, bank records, an unsworn CPA affidavit, and post-trial narrative spreadsheets, ruling: “The information in the ‘Testimony’ and ‘Explanation’ columns is not equivalent to actual testimony, and we will not rely on it.” Under I.R.C. § 446(b), the bank deposits method is a recognized, legally permissible approach for reconstructing gross income, and bank deposits constitute prima facie evidence of taxable income (Tokarski v. Commissioner, 87 T.C. 74, 77 (1986); Clayton v. Commissioner, 102 T.C. 632, 645 (1994)). In applying the method, the IRS must account for any known non-taxable sources (Clayton, 102 T.C. at 645–46). Applying these principles, the court sustained the Commissioner’s determination of $162,091 in unreported 2015 income. Regarding the $115,870.52 Porsche reimbursement, the court found that the IRS examiner had already identified this item as non-taxable in the audit schedule, meaning no adjustment was necessary. Regarding the claimed $50,000 Water Well refund, the check produced in evidence indicated “For Loan pmt” rather than a refund, and Mr. West failed to trace any corresponding deposit into his bank accounts. Thus, Mr. West failed to meet his burden of proving the BDA was inaccurate. Under I.R.C. § 162(a), taxpayers may deduct ordinary and necessary expenses paid or incurred in carrying on a trade or business, while personal living expenses (I.R.C. § 262(a)) and capital expenditures (I.R.C. § 263(a)) are strictly non-deductible. Taxpayers bear the statutory duty under I.R.C. § 6001 and Treas. Reg. § 1.6001-1(a) to maintain permanent books and records sufficient to establish deduction amounts and business purpose (Higbee v. Commissioner, 116 T.C. 438, 440 (2001)). Under the long-standing Cohan doctrine (Cohan v. Commissioner, 39 F.2d 540, 543–44 (2d Cir. 1930)), if a taxpayer proves that a deductible expenditure occurred but cannot prove the exact amount, the court may estimate the allowable deduction, bearing heavily against the non-substantiating taxpayer. However, Judge Gustafson emphasized a critical statutory limitation: the Cohan estimation doctrine does not apply to expenses governed by I.R.C. § 274(d). Citing Sanford v. Commissioner, 50 T.C. 823, 827–28 (1968), aff’d per curiam, 412 F.2d 201 (2d Cir. 1969), the court emphasized: “a court may not invoke the Cohan doctrine to estimate the amount of a deductible expense–such as travel and ‘listed property’–that is subject to the strict substantiation requirements in section 274(d), since those requirements supersede the Cohan doctrine.” Applying I.R.C. § 274(d) to Mr. West’s claimed Schedule C travel expenses (including private aircraft and helicopter flights), the court held that Mr. West failed to provide contemporaneous flight logs, travel calendars, or evidence corroborating business purpose. Furthermore, the court discovered that several travel invoices represented personal trips (including doctor visits and recreational events) or transfers between Mr. West’s own entities (BL Aviation and Q2BW). As Judge Gustafson observed: “One could say that he has proved he took money out of his left pocket and put it in his right pocket, but he has not shown that he made a deductible expenditure from his right pocket.” All disallowed travel deductions were sustained. Regarding legal and professional fees under I.R.C. § 162, the origin-of-the-claim doctrine determines deductibility (United States v. Gilmore, 372 U.S. 39, 49 (1963)). The court analyzed individual payees: For claims arising from the 2015 Asset Purchase Agreement, the court disallowed the $187,114.62 payment to QMC because the contract failed to identify the underlying business nature of the debt. Conversely, the court allowed a $112,257.21 deduction for heavy equipment repairs paid directly to Q-Haul, Inc., holding that equipment maintenance for oilfield machinery constituted a fully substantiated I.R.C. § 162 business expense. The central legal issue concerned Mr. West’s claim to a $6.8 million ordinary partnership loss carryback under I.R.C. § 704(d). Section 704(d) provides that a partner’s distributive share of partnership loss is allowable only to the extent of the partner’s adjusted basis in the partnership interest at the end of the partnership year. Under I.R.C. § 722, adjusted basis includes money and property contributed to the partnership. Because Mr. West contributed zero capital (providing only labor), his initial outside basis was zero. Mr. West argued that his execution of the $5 million CTA Note provided outside basis. The court rejected this position under settled precedent, citing VisionMonitor Software, LLC v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2014-182: “We have long held that the contribution of a partner’s own note to his partnership isn’t the equivalent of a contribution of cash, and without more, it will not increase his basis in his partnership interest.” Furthermore, the note was executed in favor of Mr. Quintanilla individually, not the partnership. The court further analyzed the “at-risk” rules under I.R.C. § 465. Under I.R.C. § 465(b)(3)(A), borrowed amounts are not considered at risk if borrowed from any person who has an interest in the activity (other than as a creditor). Because Mr. Quintanilla was a 50% co-partner in the joint venture, any liability borrowed from him was statutorily excluded from Mr. West’s at-risk amount. Additionally, under Treas. Reg. § 1.752-2(h)(4), a partner’s promissory note contributed to a partnership is disregarded for debt allocation purposes unless readily tradeable on an established securities market. Finally, the court held that the 2015 Asset Purchase Agreement did not constitute a repayment of debt under I.R.C. § 704(d) because the asset sale was a separate transaction for full consideration ($4.5 million used to settle other liabilities) and did not satisfy the CTA Note. Because Mr. West maintained a zero tax basis, Judge Gustafson held: “Mr. West cannot deduct any losses of the partnership when his basis in the partnership is zero.” Under I.R.C. § 6662(a) and (b)(2), a 20% penalty applies to underpayments attributable to a “substantial understatement of income tax” (exceeding the greater of 10% of the required tax or $5,000). Under I.R.C. § 7491(c), the Commissioner bears the burden of production regarding penalty liability and must show compliance with the supervisory approval requirement of I.R.C. § 6751(b)(1). The parties stipulated that written supervisory approval was timely secured. To avoid the penalty, the taxpayer must demonstrate “reasonable cause” and “good faith” under I.R.C. § 6664(c)(1) and Treas. Reg. § 1.6664-4. The court found that Mr. West failed to establish reasonable cause, noting that generalized claims regarding lost records, partner hostility, or unexamined document boxes do not satisfy the statutory defense. Hi CIPAWorld, grab your popcorn because we’ve got another Popa development. On October 5, 2026, the Northern District of California remanded Davis v. NerdWallet, Inc., a putative privacy class action involving website tracking technologies, back to Alameda County Superior Court after the parties agreed that the plaintiff lacked Article III standing under the Ninth Circuit’s decision in Popa v. Microsoft Corp., 153 F.4th 784 (9th Cir. 2025). Plaintiff Fatima Davis alleged that NerdWallet invaded her privacy, and the privacy of other proposed class members, through its use of website tracking technologies. Her complaint asserts claims under the California Invasion of Privacy Act (“CIPA”), the Electronic Communications Privacy Act, the California Computer Data Access and Fraud Act, the California Constitution, and California’s Unfair Competition Law. NerdWallet removed the action to federal court based on federal-question jurisdiction and the Class Action Fairness Act. Then Popa entered the picture. On September 22, the court ordered the parties to explain why Davis had Article III standing in light of the Ninth Circuit’s decision in Popa. The answer? Both parties agreed that she didn’t. Davis argued that 28 U.S.C. § 1447(c) required the action to be remanded to state court. NerdWallet, meanwhile, did not take a position on whether the appropriate result was remand or dismissal. The court sided with Davis. Under Section 1447(c), when a federal court determines that it lacks subject-matter jurisdiction before the final judgment, “the case shall be remanded.” The court also relied on Ninth Circuit precedent holding that a federal court ordinarily must remand a removed action when subject-matter jurisdiction is lacking rather than dismiss it. There is a narrow exception—but it didn’t save NerdWallet from remand. Under Ninth Circuit precedent, dismissal rather than remand may be appropriate where there is “absolute certainty” that the state court would dismiss the action following remand. The court found no such certainty here. In fact, the court pointed to another recent Northern District of California decision, Robinson v. Snap-On Inc., which likewise remanded a putative class action asserting the same claims to state court. With no basis to conclude that Alameda County Superior Court would necessarily dismiss Davis’s claims, the court remanded the case. Davis highlights an increasingly important wrinkle in the post-Popa world: a lack of Article III standing may get a CIPA defendant out of federal court without getting the defendant out of the lawsuit. For defendants removing privacy cases to federal court, a successful standing argument could be a double-edged sword. If the federal court lacks jurisdiction, Section 1447(c) may send the case right back to where it started. So while Popa continues to provide defendants with a powerful Article III argument, Davis is a reminder that winning on standing does not always mean winning the case. Sometimes, it’s just changing the courtroom. title: Honda Reportedly Delays Production of the Next-Gen CR-V Hybrid Until April 2027 - Car and Driver
content: Next-generation CR-Vs will enter production three months late, but they’ll eventually take over the Civic’s spot in Honda’s Indiana plant. The Honda CR-V is getting a major redesign for 2028, but the automaker is reportedly pushing back the start of production to make more 2027 models first. Though the delayed start date means lower output of the new CR-V in the first year, Honda is clearing space for increased production in the near future, according to a report from Automotive News. The CR-V is Honda’s most popular nameplate in the United States, making up 9.5 percent of Honda’s total U.S. sales through September this year. The Civic comes in second place, but Honda is prioritizing U.S. production of the redesigned compact SUV over its economy car in 2028. See all results for new 2026 Honda CR-V Hybrid for sale near 60629 Last year, Honda shifted a lot of its CR-V production from Canada to the United States to lower the impact of import tariffs. U.S.-market CR-Vs are now primarily built in East Liberty, Ohio, and Greensburg, Indiana. The current-generation CR-Vs are in high demand, so Honda is reportedly pushing production of the redesigned hybrid-only CR-V to April 2027 to give this year’s model a bit more production time. The delay means Honda is said to be expecting a 6.7 percent decrease in its monthly output of the redesigned model in its first year. However, that reduction will be followed by a huge production increase. The AN report says Honda is canceling its original plans to build the next-gen Civic at its Indiana plant beginning in May 2028, which gives the CR-V plenty of breathing room once the Civic moves out. The Indiana plant is projected to build around 70,000 Civics this year. Civic hatchbacks sold in North America are exclusively built in Indiana. While the next-gen Civic sedan will still be built in Canada, Honda will begin importing Civic hatchbacks from its Japanese plant once next-gen production takes over. The restructuring is part of Honda’s ambitious plan to release 15 new or heavily refreshed models globally by 2030, with an emphasis on its next-generation hybrid powertrains. Honda is reportedly planning to build another hybrid-focused assembly plant in the United States, but that space is likely claimed by its upcoming large hybrid SUV lineup. The next-generation CR-V will reportedly be sold with only a hybrid powertrain and is projected to start production in 2027 for the 2028 model year. title: Williams v. Huner - Constitutional Accountability Center
content:
In Williams v. Huner, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit is considering whether a Pennsylvania prison’s failure to provide a prisoner with rigid neck and wrist braces and effective pain medication violated the Americans with Disabilities Act. A Pennsylvania prison denied John Williams, a prisoner with neck and arm disabilities, the rigid neck brace, rigid wrist splints, and effective pain medication he needed to access prison services and activities. Absent these accommodations that immobilize his neck, hands, and wrists and manage his pain, Williams experiences debilitating pain that impedes, and at times entirely prevents, him from participating in various everyday activities like sleeping, eating, holding objects, opening doors, and cleaning himself. Title II of the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) bars discrimination by public entities, providing that “no qualified individual with a disability shall, by reason of such disability, be excluded from participation in or be denied the benefits of the services, programs, or activities of a public entity, or be subjected to discrimination by any such entity.” That bar creates an affirmative obligation on public entities to provide accommodations that allow people with disabilities to meaningfully access public services, programs, and activities. The Supreme Court has repeatedly recognized that Title II’s nondiscrimination mandate applies to all public entities, including state prisons. And the statutory text is clear: medical care is a service under Title II. Nonetheless, the district court below dismissed Williams’s failure-to-accommodate ADA claim because, it said, that claim was actually challenging inadequate medical treatment. Williams appealed, and in October 2026, CAC filed an amicus brief in the Third Circuit supporting his claim. Our brief makes three principal points. First, there is no textual carveout that excludes prison medical care from Title II’s broad prohibition on disability discrimination. Second, even if there were such a carveout, Williams’s requests were interventions to accommodate his disabilities under Title II (and thus restore his access to prison services and activities), not medical treatment at all. Third, and finally, the district court erred in invoking a line of cases stemming from a 1996 Seventh Circuit decision, Bryant v. Madigan, which first posited an atextual, “judge-made” carveout for prison medical care. That carveout is plainly at odds with Title II’s broad statutory ban on discrimination in any public “service, program, or activity.” Join CAC's Constitutional Progressives email list for updates on our work! ?

title: Wilmer's new glaucoma chief Thomas V. Johnson III on his vision - Ophthalmology Times
content: The Wilmer Eye Institute's new Glaucoma Division chief discusses mentoring junior faculty, multicenter trials, and optic nerve regeneration. Thomas V. Johnson III, MD, PhD, the Shelley and Allan Holt Rising Professor of Ophthalmology at the Wilmer Eye Institute at Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine in Baltimore, Maryland, was recently named chief of the Glaucoma Division. He is the division’s third chief, following Harry A. Quigley, MD, and Pradeep Y. Ramulu, MD, MHS, PhD. In this Q&A with Ophthalmology Times (OT), Johnson discusses his vision for the role, including mentoring junior faculty and building infrastructure for multicenter clinical trials. He also reflects on how leading residents through the early COVID-19 pandemic shaped his approach to leadership, how his work founding a community vision screening program informs his view of access to care, and how close optic nerve regeneration is to reaching patients. Note: Transcript edited lightly for clarity and length. Thomas V. Johnson III, MD, PhD: Thank you very much! Fortunately, as the third chief of the Wilmer Glaucoma Division, I am standing on the shoulders of Drs. Harry Quigley and Pradeep Ramulu, who built and led this division for many years. Together, they did an incredible job of recruiting some of the best clinicians and scientists in our field and establishing a culture of clinical excellence, scholarly rigor, and collegiality that makes this an incredible place to spend a career. So, my top priority is simply to not break anything! Beyond that however, I have two major foci at present. First is to continue building the careers of our junior faculty, five of whom completed fellowship within the past few years. Thankfully, I anticipate that this will be an easy job since they are all outstanding glaucoma physicians and brilliant scientists who are already making important contributions to the research in our field. Second, I am working to increase our infrastructure to lead multicenter clinical trials. As a glaucoma specialist and a neuroscientist, I am incredibly excited by the neuroprotective therapies coming down the R&D pipeline and I want Wilmer Eye Institute to be at the forefront of this work in the coming years. Johnson: The ACS year at Wilmer Eye Institute is a transformational experience that not only provides an opportunity for service to the institution and education for our residents, but also a unique capacity for leadership development. I think this has borne out in the sheer number of former Wilmer ACSs who have gone on to become department Chairs, society/professional organization presidents, and other prominent leaders in our field. Peter J. McDonnell, MD, our department Chair, prioritizes leadership development for our trainees and faculty, and through that I’ve read a lot about leadership styles. The one that speaks to me most directly is Servant Leadership, wherein one leads by example and serves to empower and prioritize the growth of those they are leading. I really try to embody that ethos whenever I can, and my ACS year provided a unique opportunity for this with the initial surge of the COVID-19 pandemic. As many will recall, this was a scary time when exposure to infected patients was associated with real risk; the mortality rate was significant. Nonetheless, sick patients in our hospital had to be treated and if they had an eye problem, they needed to see an ophthalmologist. During the first few weeks of the pandemic, I didn’t feel it was reasonable to subject our residents to that uncertain risk if not necessary, so I saw all of the inpatient consults myself. Fortunately, Johns Hopkins adapted to the uncertainty very quickly and put clear protocols in place to ensure the safety of all the clinical staff, so the residents were able to get back to experiential learning rather quickly. But the experience helped instill in me a mentality that a leader shouldn’t ask anyone to do something that they wouldn’t readily do themselves. Johnson: Absolutely. We started the SightSavers program (now called the Vision Screening In Our Neighborhoods or ViSION Program) in 2011 and once again, I have to credit Harry Quigley with helping to make it happen. One of our founding tenets that we continue to adhere to today is that screening for eye disease is unhelpful unless it also provides a mechanism to clinically address newly discovered pathology. I am grateful that Wilmer Eye Institute has the capacity to care for patients regardless of their insurance status or ability to pay, through a generous, anonymous philanthropic gift that we lovingly refer to as the “Angel Fund.” Through that mechanism, the ViSION program and Wilmer Eye Institute Glaucoma Faculty have the ability not to worry about insurance reimbursement and instead focus on the care of the patients in our clinics and operating rooms. Putting the patient first has always been a central part of the Wilmer Eye Institute culture, and I certainly intend to continue fostering that mentality as glaucoma chief. Johnson: I am tremendously excited for the future of regenerative medicine in ophthalmology and in glaucoma specifically. While restoring vision to people who are blind from glaucoma through optic nerve regeneration has been a distant dream for decades, it is clear to me that neuroscience, stem cell biology, molecular biology, and biomedical engineering have advanced to the point that restoring lost sight will be possible. I think the scientific community is recognizing that, too, and the enthusiasm of the more than 300 international members of the RGC Repopulation, Stem Cell Transplantation, and Optic Nerve Regeneration (RReSTORe) Consortium underscores that point. In our own laboratories, we are now able to take human stem cell derived retinal ganglion cells, transplant them into the eyes of preclinical models of glaucoma, and observe not only functional (synaptic) connectivity in the retina but axonal growth through the optic nerve and into the brain. I think that full-length anterior visual pathway regeneration in animal models is just around the corner. That said, it is always challenging to predict how long this will take to translate to human patients, and a first-in-human clinical trial likely remains several years away. At this point, the biggest hurdle is going to be increasing the efficiency of RGC replacement from a few hundred neurons to tens of thousands—a number that will ultimately be required to restore a meaningful level of vision to patients blind from glaucoma and other optic neuropathies. Johnson: Continued success for the Wilmer Eye Institute glaucoma division will involve first and foremost, maintaining our leadership in clinical excellence, education, and vision research. Beyond that, I strive to continue mentoring and helping to build the careers of our junior faculty. For some, that will mean developing and growing a clinical and research program at Wilmer Eye Institute and for others that will mean taking on new leadership opportunities outside our institution. Indeed, while we were terribly sad for ourselves to see Pradeep Ramulu move to become the Chair at Bascom Palmer Eye Institute, we also recognize that such a transition to a prominent leadership role is exactly what our institution and our glaucoma division are all about: cultivating and building clinical, educational, research, and leadership excellence so that we can impact our field beyond the walls of our own institution. title: Cornel West keynotes Black Men's Legacy Summit V - Insight News
content:
Partly cloudy. Low near 45F. Winds light and variable.. Partly cloudy. Low near 45F. Winds light and variable. As the 2026 midterm elections approach, the U.S. Supreme Cou… Both directions of Interstate 94 through the Lowry Hill Tunn… Black men will gather in Minneapolis Oct. 31 for the fifth annual Black Men’s Legacy Summit, a day organizers are framing around a central question: What legacy are families and communities building for the generations that follow? Presented by 9000 Equities, the summit will run from 10 a.m. to 3 p.m., with doors opening at 9:30 a.m., at the Regional Access Center, 1256 Penn Ave. N., fifth floor, in Minneapolis. Admission is free and open to the public, with space limited and available on a first-come, first-served basis. This year’s theme, “Legacy Under Fire—Stand Your Ground,” places the focus on preserving what earlier generations built while creating new opportunities for those coming behind them. Organizers list six topics for the day: Black fathers and their sons; youth; the Collective Kitchen; economic opportunity; health and wellness; and politics and legacy. Dr. Cornel West, the scholar, author and public philosopher, will deliver the keynote address, “The State of the Nation.” Organizers say his address will examine DEI, voting power and access to ownership. West is the Dietrich Bonhoeffer Professor of Philosophy and Christian Practice at Union Theological Seminary and professor emeritus at Princeton University. He earned his doctorate in philosophy from Princeton in 1980 and is the author of numerous books, including Race Matters, Democracy Matters and Black Prophetic Fire. The program connects family relationships with questions of ownership and long-term community capacity. The Black Fathers and Their Sons topic will focus on strengthening relationships, responsibility, mentorship and what one generation passes to the next. A youth topic, “Next In Line: Our Turn to Build,” will bring younger participants into conversations about opportunity, leadership, wealth and the futures they want to create. The Collective Kitchen will explore connection and collaboration and what organizers describe as the potential created when people work together to strengthen families and communities. Economic questions will receive a dedicated topic, “Thriving Economic Opportunities to Build Legacies.” The announced discussion includes ownership, entrepreneurship, homeownership and other pathways toward long-term wealth building. The “Health is Wealth” topic broadens that discussion by examining health, wellness and longevity as components of sustaining a legacy. Another topic, “Politics and Legacy,” will focus on civic engagement and policy and on how decisions made today can affect families, communities, ownership and opportunity across generations. Taken together, the six topics give the summit’s use of the word “legacy” a practical meaning. The agenda moves from relationships inside families to health, economic participation, ownership and civic engagement, treating each as part of what can be built and transferred from one generation to another. That emphasis on practical outcomes mirrors the mission of Build Wealth MN, the nonprofit that created the 9000 Equities initiative with partners. Founded in 2004, Build Wealth MN describes its work as helping people develop new approaches to giving, saving, banking, investing, homeownership and the creation of generational wealth. According to the organization, it has served thousands of clients and supported more than 7,000 families in attaining homeownership since its founding. Its programs include the Family Stabilization Plan, Youth Stabilization Program, Rent Smart-Wise and Ready, PEEP (Pathways to Increase Employment and Earnings Potential), mortgage loans and down payment assistance, and housing development. Homeownership is also central to the work of 9000 Equities. According to 9000 Equities, the initiative is working with partners toward financing 9,000 new Black homeowners over five to seven years, with a stated objective of reducing Minnesota’s homeownership gap by 15 percent. Those figures are the initiative’s own targets. The state data behind that target is stark. A March 2025 report from the Minnesota State Demographic Center found that Black homeownership in Minnesota is less than half the statewide rate of 72 percent, while white homeownership is 77 percent. The report, written by demographer Jeff Howison, found that the rate for Black households has fallen by about one-third since 1970 and declined in every decade since the 1960s except the 1990s. Black homeowners grew from 4,338 to 30,544 between 1970 and 2020, while Black renters grew from 6,027 to 94,488. Some newer immigrant communities have made modest gains, the report says, but U.S.-born African Americans have not. One-year Census data for 2023 showed Black homeownership rising to 32 percent, a change the report’s long-term figures do not capture. The Council for Minnesotans of African Heritage, a state council created by the Legislature to advise the governor and lawmakers, has pointed to the same gap. In a March 2025 factsheet supporting a proposed Black homeownership program, the council said fewer than 30 percent of Black Minnesotans own their homes and that 60 percent of Black Minnesotans pay more than they can afford for housing, compared with 30 percent of all Minnesota households. At the federal level, the Trump administration’s Department of Housing and Urban Development proposed in January to repeal its Fair Housing Act regulations on disparate impact, the standard for challenging housing practices that disadvantage a protected group even without proof of discriminatory intent. HUD said the change would leave questions about that liability to the courts, and it cited an April 2025 executive order stating that the law guarantees “equality of opportunity, not outcomes.” HUD’s notice acknowledges the Supreme Court’s 2015 ruling that disparate-impact claims are allowed under the Fair Housing Act, and it says the proposal changes no rights or obligations. In August, HUD added a supplemental proposal covering its Title VI rules for recipients of federal housing aid and reopened public comment on the January proposal. The Justice Department finalized a similar change to its own Title VI rules in December 2025, HUD’s August notice says. HUD has been direct about its aim. Secretary Scott Turner wrote in a Jan. 19 National Review column that HUD is moving to end the agency’s use of disparate-impact theory in fair housing and related civil rights enforcement. HUD’s notice says the change would not alter any rights or obligations and that courts, not a federal agency, should determine how disparate-impact liability is interpreted. HUD has also turned its attention to Minneapolis. In a Jan. 15 letter to Mayor Jacob Frey, Craig Trainor, HUD’s assistant secretary for fair housing, opened an investigation into whether the city’s housing policies violate the Fair Housing Act and Title VI of the Civil Rights Act. The letter opens with allegations of fraud involving Minnesota’s Somali community and says what it calls racial favoritism “appears to extend to Minneapolis’s housing policy.” It points to the Minneapolis 2040 plan’s priority for cultural districts, the plan’s pledge to focus on people of color and Indigenous people in expanding support for homeowners, and a city department’s plan to prioritize rental housing for communities of color and immigrants. Turner said the agency would not stand for racial and ethnic preferences. A city spokesperson said the investigation appears to be “about politics, not affordable housing.” The proposal drew organized opposition. The Legal Defense Fund, known as LDF, the civil rights law organization founded in 1940, told HUD in a Feb. 13 comment that the agency was abdicating its duty to fight housing discrimination. Demetria McCain, LDF’s director of policy, said the attacks on disparate impact are “part of the administration’s broader efforts to undermine civil rights law.” She added that HUD itself concedes courts still recognize such claims. The National Fair Housing Alliance led a coalition of 174 civil rights, fair housing and fair lending organizations in urging HUD not to finalize the change. Nikitra Bailey, the alliance’s executive vice president, said the Supreme Court has already made clear that disparate impact is recognized under the Fair Housing Act. The alliance said its campaign helped drive 1,426 comments filed with HUD. The ACLU and the Impact Fund told HUD in a Feb. 12 comment that the proposal conflicts with the Supreme Court’s 2015 ruling, disregards the reliance that people and institutions have placed on the rule for more than a decade, and allowed only 30 days for comment when HUD’s own policy calls for 60. The ACLU cited its analysis finding that landlords filed eviction cases against Black renters at more than twice the rate they did against white renters from 2012 to 2016. LeadingAge, which represents more than 5,400 aging-services providers, also urged HUD to keep the rules, saying their removal would reduce protections for older adults. Comment on HUD’s August proposal closes Oct. 9. The stakes are concrete for Black homeowners. On Jan. 12, the Supreme Court declined to hear an appeal by Emigrant Bank and Emigrant Mortgage Company, leaving in place a jury verdict that awarded $722,000 in compensatory damages to eight New York homeowners. Their lawyers said the bank marketed high-cost refinance loans, issued between 1999 and 2008, to Black and Latino homeowners with poor credit and significant equity, and that the borrowers lost that equity and, in some cases, their homes. According to the ACLU, the bank had asked the justices to consider whether the 2015 ruling recognizing disparate-impact claims “has proven unworkable.” The Court denied the petition without explanation. For the summit, the debate lands close to home. Its theme, “Legacy Under Fire—Stand Your Ground,” is about protecting what earlier generations built while creating opportunity for those who follow. The Fair Housing Act of 1968 is one of those inheritances, and disparate impact is one of the tools used to enforce it. Organizers describe the Politics and Legacy topic as exploring how decisions made today affect ownership and opportunity across generations. HUD’s proposal is one such decision. In the summit’s terms, the work has two fronts: building ownership, as 9000 Equities aims to do, and defending the rules that protect that ownership from discrimination. Organizers say the objective of the summit is not simply to talk about legacy but to help Black men identify practical pathways to build, protect and sustain wealth and opportunity for their families and communities. Participants will be encouraged to connect with resources and consider how ideas discussed during the summit can be turned into action afterward. For organizers, the summit connects the immediate work of strengthening families with the longer work of building ownership and assets that can move from one generation to the next. Registration for Black Men’s Legacy Summit V is open through Eventbrite. The event is free and open to the public, although space is limited. title: Spotify, Apple Music and Others Respond to Phono V Rate Proposal - Digital Music News
content: We exclusively broke down that proposal yesterday, when the Songwriters Guild of America, Word Collections, and several others formally called for a flat mechanical rate of $0.003 per on-demand stream during 2028 with annual inflation adjustments to follow. The proposal, which would make for a dramatically simpler system in part by preventing royalty-reducing “bundling” shenanigans, didn’t arrive out of left field. As many know, Spotify reclassified the vast majority of its stateside subscriptions as bundles, thereby reaping massive mechanicals savings. Against this backdrop, Spotify’s subsequent direct deals aside, the possibility of another years-long rate-setting showdown has been looming large for some time. Back in 2024, for instance, National Music Publishers’ Association (NMPA) head David Israelite indicated that Spotify “should go ahead and block your calendar for that trial,” with the DSP having “lost the ability to enter into good-faith negotiations with us.” And it was only earlier this year that the NMPA pointed to almost $500 million in axed mechanicals as a result of Spotify’s bundling craze. Throw in noticeable (albeit less aggressive) bundling reclassifications at Amazon Music and Apple Music, and the stage may well be set for a Phono V showdown. Publishing revenue has risen substantially in recent years, and notwithstanding their differences, the involved parties should huddle together and reach an agreement as opposed to locking horns for years to come, DIMA president and CEO Graham Davies appeared to relay in more words. “Yesterday, the parties to the Phonorecords V proceeding submitted their written testimony and rate proposals to the Copyright Royalty Board,” Davies stated. “In this proceeding, which takes place every five years, the CRB will determine the mechanical royalty rates paid by music streaming services in the United States for the years 2028-2032. In the last proceeding, which concluded in 2022, publishers and DSPs reached a settlement, securing rates for 2023-2027 and laying the groundwork for future growth. “According to the NMPA, U.S. music publishing revenues have grown more than 30% since 2022, from $5.6 billion to $7.3 billion, outpacing the growth of recorded music, and music streaming has continued to innovate and thrive. DIMA joins its member companies in looking forward to a timely resolution of this proceeding, and to continue building on the success of streaming for rights owners, music creators, and DSPs alike,” he finished. So is the conspicuous absence of any comments whatsoever concerning the substance of the Phono V proposal, which would represent a significant shift from the current model. Though DIMA itself opted against weighing in on the actual proposal text, DSPs themselves submitted all manner of written statements to the CRB. Also brewing is a sub-dispute over the NMPA’s aggressive attempt to subpoena pertinent documents from the Mechanical Licensing Collective v. Spotify legal battle. Put differently, depending on one’s perspective, the rate-setting proceeding might have already transformed into an all-out showdown, and it’ll be worth closely tracking the approaching weeks’ and months’ Phono V submissions.

title: Inside New Noise: V of BTS, Kelela, Navy Blue, and Nothing betting culture beats capital - Yahoo Creators
content: Nothing is a six-year-old startup from London picking a fight with Sony, Apple, and Bose. Barely a week ago, it made its case at HERO in Rockefeller Center, where "New Noise" doubled as a product launch and a statement of intent: a "future of sound" roundtable with Kelela and Navy Blue, a live set from Navy Blue and his tour DJ AWHLEE, and two announcements, the Headphone (1) Pro, the company's new flagship and most advanced audio product to date, and V of BTS as its newest Global Brand Ambassador, fronting a campaign shot in Seoul by Dorothea Sing Zhang that premiered in the room. After the panel, I sat down with the two executives carrying the night: Philipp Von Lintel, Nothing's Lead Industrial Designer, and Charlie Smith, its Chief Brand Officer. Shavone Charles is the company's Global Head of Communications, and she moderated the artist conversation. The throughline of every conversation was a hierarchy the tech industry usually flips. The technology is good, and it is deliberately not the point. Artistry first, community second, specs somewhere after that. It showed up in the product, in the programming, and in the initiatives Nothing is funding. For a six-year-old startup picking a fight with Sony, Apple, and Bose, and by its own telling the only new smartphone maker to emerge in the last decade, it's also the only play available: it can't outspend the giants, so it's trying to out-care them. Von Lintel calls the Pro an evolution of last year's Headphone (1) with one sharp turn. The design language carries over, but everything reoriented once engineering cracked something new on sound. "We started the design around the sound," he told me. Part of the push came from inside the building: engineers and designers on the team make music themselves, and they needed headphones they could actually work in. So Nothing built the pair its own people were asking for. That inside-out logic is visible in the hardware. Nothing exposes its engineering instead of hiding it, which Von Lintel compared to "having an open kitchen in a restaurant." It makes his job harder in the most literal way. He described a two-week standoff with engineers over the center driver sitting a couple of millimeters too low to look right. The verdict from design: it doesn't fly. They moved it. The Pro also keeps the physical controls that became the first model's signature quirk: a roller, a paddle, a button, in a market where everyone else does tap and swipe. Von Lintel says the feedback has been emphatic, mostly from people thrilled to skip tracks without digging out their phones. And it keeps a 3.5mm jack, pitched as a working musician's feature. DJ with them. Plug in a CD player. Use them on a plane without buying a dongle. While the rest of tech keeps sanding features down to nothing, Von Lintel argued, strip out enough and eventually there's hardly anything left. Every one of those calls puts the musician before the margin. If Von Lintel sweats how the thing feels, Smith sweats what it means. Asked what Nothing does differently from Sony, Apple, and Bose, he skipped the spec sheet entirely. "I genuinely don't believe that there are other headphone brands out there who are connecting to music culture in the way that we do," he said. Then the night's best unscripted moment. Smith started to say "I mean, who has Charli?" and the room tilted, because his name is Charlie. Charli xcx, who joined Nothing as Global Brand Ambassador and shareholder this spring, was in Smith's very first brand strategy deck before he even joined the company. She is his working definition of "rebellious creativity," and he was quick to say what it isn't: not punk, no spiky hair and nose ring. It's countercultural, railing against the fake perfection of social media, the matcha latte pilates aesthetic, in favor of something rawer. "Brat is like a strappy top, no bra, pack of fags, and a bit of glitter," he said. "It's this kind of raw authenticity." The philosophy is turning into line items. Smith pointed to the Nothing Fund, which puts money directly into the hands of grassroots promoters putting on live music, and to a customer base with an average age of 27. The company is building for Gen Z and Gen Alpha on purpose. "We want to uplift music culture and leave it in a better place than when we started," he said. Pressed for the most rebellious thing Nothing has done on his watch, Smith went back to first principles. Rebellion is forging your own path while everyone else ships the predictable thing. His favorite example isn't a tech company at all. It's Lyas, the 26-year-old French influencer behind fashion's viral "Watch Party" movement. Turned away from a Dior show, Lyas livestreamed it from a Paris bar instead, and a thousand students showed up, Smith said. Months later he was packing the Théâtre du Châtelet with thousands of young fans watching the shows together. "He was a rock star," Smith said. "You can kind of predict what the products are going to be that tech companies are going to launch now," he added. "It's like with Apple launching, everyone knew what it was going to be. Another phone, another phone, another phone." His closing argument: "If we could really become this tech company for the next generation and be part of a new, different, optimistic vision of the future, then to me, that's the biggest act of rebellion in the world." The team itself makes the argument. Nothing's lead designer came from furniture, lighting, and music instruments. Its brand chief came from luxury fashion. Its communications chief is a classically trained flautist who ran music culture at Twitter, Instagram, and TikTok. "We have a lot of outside perspectives that are really questioning and challenging the status quo," Von Lintel said. "That diversity of thought is what creates the richness of the brand." The programming made the same argument as the product. Charles said Kelela and Navy Blue were the right voices for the panel because "[both are] groundbreaking artists who don't follow trends, instead following their internal inspiration wherever it takes them. They emphasize their humanity and vulnerability in their art, even as they create unique sonic worlds." On what she listens for in headphones: "The combination of comfort, stylistic expression, and audio fidelity that Nothing offers is second-to-none... Nothing specializes in a functional and absorbing listening experience that eliminates the distance between you and your favorite music." Kelela and Navy Blue are the headline, but they're not the whole story. They're the proof of concept. Artists who don't follow trends don't show up for companies that do. Can caring about the culture beat outspending everyone in it? That's Nothing's wager. On a Monday night in Rockefeller Center, with Kelela talking process and Navy Blue performing, it looked less like a marketing strategy than a point of view. title: V. James DeSimone Law Welcomes Nikhil Ramnaney as Of Counsel - Legal Reader
content: Ramnaney, a former federal civil rights prosecutor and longtime public defender, brings insight into how government agencies investigate, and defend, claims of law enforcement misconduct. MARINA DEL REY, Calif. — V. James DeSimone Law, a Southern California employment and civil rights firm, announced that trial attorney Nikhil Ramnaney, of Harbor Justice Law, has joined the firm as of counsel. He will work with V. James DeSimone Law’s civil rights team on cases involving police misconduct, employment discrimination and other civil rights actions. This includes all violations of constitutional rights such as excessive force, wrongful death, and malicious prosecution. Nikhil will continue his work as a preeminent criminal defense attorney taking on select matters in state and federal court. For more than four decades, civil rights attorney V. James DeSimone has successfully represented individuals and families who have suffered harm at the hands of law enforcement, government entities, businesses and other powerful institutions. “Nikhil has seen this work from every angle,” DeSimone said. “His range of experience makes him a fierce advocate for people who have been harmed by the institutions meant to protect them. We’re grateful to have him on our team.” Ramnaney spent several years as a trial attorney in the Civil Rights Division of the U.S. Department of Justice. Working out of Justice Department headquarters in Washington, D.C., he investigated and prosecuted police and correctional officers accused of abuse of authority, violence, and obstruction of justice. His cases took him across the country and included investigations into in-custody deaths and physical abuse inside correctional facilities. He received multiple commendations from the FBI and the U.S. Attorney General for that work. Before joining the Justice Department, Ramnaney represented public entities and law enforcement agencies in civil litigation, including police-related employment disputes and internal investigations. That work gave him firsthand knowledge of how municipalities and law enforcement agencies investigate officer misconduct, handle internal discipline and defend civil lawsuits. He now uses that inside knowledge on behalf of plaintiffs. As a Los Angeles County Public Defender, Ramnaney represented juveniles and adults on charges ranging from misdemeanors to homicide. Over his career, he has tried nearly 50 cases and litigated hundreds of motions. He is the former president of Local 148, the Los Angeles County Public Defenders Union, and has long been an advocate for workers’ rights, organized labor, and the fair treatment of working people. “From the Department of Justice to Los Angeles courtrooms, my career has taken me from prosecuting civil rights cases to defending people facing state and federal criminal charges,” Ramnaney said. “After trying more than 50 cases, that journey has shaped how I think about the criminal justice system and police procedure, and what it takes to win. I’m excited to bring that experience to VJD Law alongside Jim, Carmen, and this team of skilled litigators and fighters. I’m ready to help deliver justice for our clients.” Born and raised in Southern California, Ramnaney earned his undergraduate degree from UCLA and then attended Tulane University Law School on an academic scholarship, graduating magna cum laude. During law school, he gained courtroom and defense experience with the Federal Public Defender’s Office, then later worked at an Am Law 100 firm handling complex, high-stakes commercial litigation for Fortune 500 companies. He is affiliated with the National Police Accountability Project, the National Association of Criminal Defense Lawyers, California Attorneys for Criminal Justice, California Public Defenders Association and the California Appellate Project – Los Angeles. He also serves on the board of the South Asian Bar Association. For more than 40 years, founder V. James DeSimone has represented individuals and employees throughout Southern California in civil rights, employment, wrongful death and catastrophic injury cases. The Marina del Rey, Calif., firm has secured multiple multi-million-dollar settlements and verdicts on behalf of its clients, and DeSimone has been recognized as a Top 100 Super Lawyer, California Civil Rights Lawyer of the Year and a Best Lawyers Civil Rights Lawyer of the Year. title: V Modern Italian, led by Michelin-starred chef, opens in North Hyde Park - Creative Loafing Tampa Bay
content:
NoHo will finally get a glimpse of Michelin-starred Chef Stefano Ciotti’s latest concept, V Modern Italian. Located at 1701 W North A St. in a 7,400 square-foot space within the new Rome Collective development, V Modern Italian will officially start taking reservations this Thursday, Oct. 8. “Guests can expect a menu rooted in authenticity, featuring antipasti, fresh-made pastas, signature entrées, and fun twists on classic Italian desserts. Familiar Italian flavors are reimagined through seasonal ingredients, thoughtful presentation, and contemporary technique,” says a press release. V Modern Italian seems to have quite a few “elevated” dishes, like the “Tutti Antipasti Tower,” which is described as a three-level structure consisting of “chef-curated antipasti.” There’s also a Martini Tower,” featuring twelve Espresso or Dirty Martinis served for the table,” and a six drink “Cocktail Carousel.” “My goal with V has always been to take everything I love about classic Italian cuisine and make it feel fresh and exciting again,” says Ciotti in a statement. “The menu respects the traditions and flavors that define Italian cooking while giving guests something unexpected to discover. Tampa has an exciting and evolving culinary scene, and we’re looking forward to becoming part of it.” V Modern Italian is open Monday-Wednesday from  4 p.m.-11 p.m., Thursday from  4 p.m.-midnight, Fridays from  4 p.m.-1 a.m., Saturdays from 3 p.m.-1 a.m. and Sundays from 3 p.m.-11 p.m. Pitch in to help make the Tampa Bay Journalism Project a success. title: Down Premiere “The Myth” Video From Upcoming Album ‘Volume V’ - The Mosh Network
content: Down have officially released their new single “The Myth,” along with a new music video for the track. The song serves as the latest preview of the NOLA supergroup’s long-awaited new album ‘Volume V’, which is due out November 20. The upcoming 10-track effort will mark Down’s first proper full-length addition to their catalog since the band completed their two-part EP series in 2014. MetalDave Media directed the newly released video, while the members of Down offered their own takes on the new track. Vocalist Phil Anselmo pointed to the song’s classic influences, particularly Trouble, while also citing legendary vocalists including James Dewar, Ronnie James Dio, Ozzy Osbourne and Glenn Hughes. “‘The Myth’ has some epic moments. It’s a jammer. It’s got a big nod to Trouble, but vocally I’m thinking of James Dewar, Ronnie James Dio, Ozzy Osbourne, Glenn Hughes, and many of the other greats.” Guitarist Kirk Windstein called the track an example of the collaborative approach that has long defined Down, while fellow guitarist Pepper Keenan described it as a classic Down track that eventually ventures into a ’70s-inspired jam. Bassist Pat Bruders noted that “The Myth” came together particularly naturally once the band were working on it collectively, while drummer Jimmy Bower singled it out as one of his favorite songs on the forthcoming record. Down currently have several live appearances scheduled, including the Pantera-led The Great NOLA Trendkill festival. title: New creative team at 180heartbeats + Jung v Matt: Justyna Sokołowska and Mateusz Vlahos join as Creative Leads - Roastbrief US
content:
October, 2026.- Sokołowska and Vlahos have worked together on projects for brands including Netflix, Żabka, PlayStation, ING and McDonald’s. They created Żabka’s “Sąsiedzi” platform and worked on campaigns for Netflix’s The Mire and PlayStation’s “Every Dad Is a Demigod”. Before joining 180heartbeats + Jung v Matt, they worked as a creative duo at DDB Warsaw and later at GONG, creating work that connected brands with wider cultural conversations. “Justyna and Mateusz bring different but highly complementary creative perspectives to the team. Mateusz has a strong feel for pop culture and storytelling, while Justyna brings a strong visual sensibility that she also develops outside advertising through painting and book illustration. As technology increasingly changes the way communication is created, we want 180’s creative work to be built around individual perspective and imagination” – says Marcin Talarek, Chief Creative Officer at 180heartbeats + Jung v Matt.Justyna Sokołowska has nearly 20 years of experience in the creative industry. Before joining 180heartbeats + Jung v Matt, she worked at GONG, DDB Warsaw (now TBWA\Warsaw), PZL and Badi Badi studio. She graduated from the Faculty of Graphic Arts at the Academy of Fine Arts in Warsaw. Outside advertising, Sokołowska works as an illustrator and painter. She has illustrated several books and exhibited her work as part of a number of art projects. Her series The History of Jews from Podlasie in Double-Warp Weaving won third prize in the Main Exhibition at the 2021 International Print Triennial in Kraków. Mateusz Vlahos has worked in advertising for 10 years. He began his career at DDB Warsaw (now TBWA\Warsaw) before moving to GONG, where he spent the past several years. He studied Film and Television at London Metropolitan University. Pop culture and cinema are among his main sources of inspiration in his creative work. He also wrote the screenplay for a short film promoting Tymek’s album Romantyk, which was awarded at KTR. title: Endeavor Catalyst Closes Oversubscribed $320 Million Fund V - Pulse 2.0
content: Endeavor Catalyst has closed an oversubscribed $320 million Fund V as the global venture investment organization increases its activity in Europe. The new fund brings Endeavor Catalyst to more than $850 million in assets under management. Europe has become the organization’s fastest-growing investment market. Endeavor Catalyst has made more than 90 investments across 10 European markets, and 20 of its European portfolio companies are valued at $1 billion or more. Fund V investments connected to Europe already include EnduroSat, founded in Bulgaria, and HappyRobot, founded by Spanish entrepreneurs. Other European portfolio companies include Bending Spoons, ElevenLabs, Preply, ICEYE and Fever. Endeavor Catalyst invested in 12 companies selected through its European offices during the first half of 2026, compared with 14 during all of 2025 and seven in 2024. Its European portfolio companies raised $3.3 billion in funding rounds joined by Endeavor Catalyst across 2025 and the first half of 2026. The organization is active across Bulgaria, Greece, Ireland, Italy, Poland, Portugal, Romania, Spain, Turkey and Ukraine. Its Global Hub in London, launched in 2024, now includes more than 90 Endeavor Entrepreneurs and 100 companies. “The talent coming out of countries like Poland, Ukraine, Romania, Greece, Spain and Turkey is some of the best anywhere in the world. We are doubling down on Europe with Fund V to help ensure European founders have access to the capital they need to build the next generation of global companies.” Pete Benedetto, Head of Europe for Endeavor Catalyst “London attracts founders who have already started building somewhere else and need a platform to take it global. They arrive with traction and the resilience of building where there was no playbook, and here they find the later-stage capital, talent and partners to scale. Fund V puts more of that capital within reach, and our role is to keep every founder one introduction away from the people who can help them build category-defining companies.” Constanza Castro Feijoo, Managing Director of Endeavor’s Global Hub in London Thank you for visiting Pulse 2.0. title: Eagles trade C Cam Jurgens before Week 5 game v. Jaguars - Yahoo Sports
content: The Philadelphia Eagles' offensive line will look quite different for Sunday's matchup with the Jacksonville Jaguars. After right tackle Lane Johnson announced his retirement on Tuesday, the Eagles are now trading center Cam Jurgens to the Baltimore Ravens for future draft capital. Jurgens was a second-round pick by the Eagles in the 2022 NFL draft and has made 45 starts in his career. He is a two-time Pro Bowler as well. Projected to take over for Jurgens is Drew Kendall, a fifth-round pick in the 2025 NFL draft, who has appeared in 11 games, making four starts.
